name: Gaura Parva
when: Bhadra, usually late August or early September (lunar dates)
summary: Gaura Parva is the great festival of Nepal's far west, celebrating the marriage of the goddess Gaura, or Parvati, to Shiva. Over four main days, married women fast, soak five grains, build an image of Gaura from plants and dance Deuda in every village of Sudurpashchim and parts of Karnali.
body: Ask anyone from Doti, Achham, Bajhang or Baitadi which festival defines their home, and most will say Gaura. It honours Gaura, the local name of Gauri or Parvati, daughter of Himavan, the Himalaya, and therefore, people say, a daughter of these hills. The festival celebrates her penance and her marriage to Shiva, and women pray to her for the health and long life of their husbands and families. It is also celebrated in the Kumaon hills of Uttarakhand, where it is called Saton–Athon.

Preparations begin days ahead, when women collect red clay and paint the ritual spaces of the house. On Biruda Panchami, the fifth day of the lunar fortnight, married women fast and soak five kinds of grain, the biruda, in a brass or bronze pot. On the sixth day they wash the grains at a spring or river, singing Deuda. On Saptami they bring plants from the fields to a chosen home, the Gaura Ghar, and make an image of the goddess from them, dressed in red cloth.

The eighth day, Gaurashtami or Athebali, is the climax. Women gather at the Gaura khalo, the festival ground, fasting and singing. An image of Shiva, Maheshwar, is made, and the two images are married in a joyful ceremony. Women carry the deities on their heads and dance, the soaked biruda is shared as blessed food, and married women put on a sacred thread. Above all there is Deuda: long lines of men and women, arms linked, singing in call and answer late into the night.
tips: Gaura is a family and village festival, so the best way to see it is through a local guide or host family in the hills of Achham, Doti or Bajhang.
Ask before photographing women during rituals and fasting, and never step over ritual objects or the Gaura images.
Gaura falls in the monsoon, so expect rain and rough roads; in Kathmandu you can also see Deuda at Tundikhel on the final day.

faqs.a: Gaura Parva falls in the Nepali month of Bhadra, usually in late August or early September. It is a lunar festival: the main days run from Biruda Panchami to Gaurashtami, and astrologers fix the dates each year, sometimes in the bright and sometimes in the dark half of the month. Check current status before you travel.

Mainly in Sudurpashchim Province, in districts such as Doti, Achham, Bajhang, Bajura, Baitadi, Dadeldhura and Darchula, and in parts of Karnali Province. It is also celebrated in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand, India. Far western communities in Kathmandu gather at Tundikhel on the final day to dance Deuda.

Yes, as respectful guests. Visitors are often welcomed to watch the Deuda dancing and the wedding of Gaura and Maheshwar, and sometimes invited to join the circle. The fasting and core rituals are for local women, so observe quietly and follow your hosts' lead. A local guide makes the experience much richer.

faqs.q: What is Deuda and why is it part of Gaura?
faqs.a: Deuda is the song and dance of the far west, sung without instruments by men and women who link arms in a circle and answer each other's verses. It is the heart of Gaura celebrations, performed when women wash the grains and on the main day. Tradition says it began in the Khasa court of Sinja.

name: Ganga Dashahara Mela at Khaptad
when: Jestha Shukla Dashami, late May or June (lunar date)
summary: Every year on Ganga Dashahara, thousands of pilgrims from Bajhang, Bajura, Achham and Doti climb to Triveni in Khaptad National Park. They sing Deuda through the night, bathe at the confluence at dawn, offer rites for their ancestors and join a fair of games, horse races and music on the high meadows.
body: Ganga Dashahara marks the descent of the Ganges from heaven to earth and falls on the tenth day of the bright half of the month of Jestha, usually in late May or June. Across South Asia Hindus bathe in sacred rivers on this day. In Nepal's far west, the great gathering is at Triveni, a confluence of streams on the Khaptad plateau, where the four districts of Bajhang, Bajura, Achham and Doti meet.

Pilgrims start climbing the day before, walking for hours from the villages below with food, blankets and offerings. On the eve of the festival the meadows fill with camps and fires, and the night belongs to Deuda: circles of men and women from different districts singing verses at each other until dawn. Then people bathe in the cold water at Triveni, worship at the temple and the lingas, and offer tarpan, rites for their ancestors, believing the day's bath washes away sins.

Alongside the worship, the fair has a festive side: volleyball competitions, horse racing on the open grass, cultural programmes and stalls. The Nepal Army post in the park and local organisers help manage the crowds, and health camps are sometimes run for pilgrims. For a visitor, it is a rare chance to see the far west's communities gathered in one place, high above their villages.
tips: Book camping support well ahead; Khaptad's single lodge and pilgrim shelters fill completely at the fair.
Reach the plateau a day early so you can acclimatise and find a good camp before the crowds arrive.
Pay the national park fee and walk with a licensed guide; check current status before you travel for the exact date.

faqs.q: When is the Ganga Dashahara fair at Khaptad?
faqs.a: It is held on Jestha Shukla Dashami, the tenth day of the bright half of Jestha, which usually falls in late May or June. Pilgrims arrive the day before and stay through the night. The date follows the lunar calendar and changes each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at the Khaptad fair?
faqs.a: Pilgrims sing Deuda through the night, bathe at Triveni at dawn, worship at the temple and lingas, and offer tarpan for their ancestors. The fair also includes volleyball, horse racing, cultural programmes and stalls. Thousands come from Bajhang, Bajura, Achham and Doti.

faqs.q: How do I reach the fair at Khaptad?
faqs.a: Fly to Dhangadhi, travel by road to a trailhead such as Meltadi in Bajhang or the Jhingrana side in Doti, and walk four to eight hours up to the plateau. Allow at least two days from Dhangadhi. Roads and flights in the far west change often; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there accommodation during the Khaptad fair?
faqs.a: Very little. The single lodge near the park office and the pilgrim shelters are packed, and most pilgrims sleep in the open or in tents. Foreign visitors should come on a supported camping trek with tents, food and a cook, booked well in advance.

name: Badimalika Janai Purnima Mela
when: Janai Purnima, full moon of Shrawan, usually August (lunar date)
summary: On Janai Purnima, thousands of pilgrims walk for days to the Badimalika temple at about 4,220 m in Bajura, where Sati's left shoulder is believed to have fallen. They bathe at Triveni, climb to the shrine, renew sacred threads and sing Deuda through the night on the high pastures.
body: Janai Purnima, the full moon of the month of Shrawan, is when Hindu men across Nepal change the sacred thread, janai, and many people tie a protective thread on the wrist. In the far west it is also the day of the greatest pilgrimage of the year, to Badimalika, the mountain goddess of Bajura, whose temple stands on a ridge at about 4,220 m. Malika Chaturdashi, on the eve of the full moon, is the temple's main festival.

Pilgrims set out days before from Bajura, Achham, Kalikot, Jumla and beyond, walking from roadheads such as Martadi through villages and forest to Triveni Dham, where three streams meet. There they camp, bathe and prepare offerings, then climb in the dark to reach the temple. The two priests of Badimalika, one from Kalikot and one from Bajura, receive offerings of flowers, coconuts, red cloth and coins.

Around the temple and at Triveni, temporary tea shops under tarpaulin sell tea, noodles and snacks, and the nights are filled with Deuda, sung in circles on the cold grass. The fair falls in the monsoon, with rain, mist and mud, but the devotion of the crowds and the setting far above the tree line make it one of the most remarkable gatherings in the Himalaya.
tips: Start the trek from Martadi at least four days before the full moon to arrive acclimatised and unhurried.
Bring full rain gear, a strong tent and a four-season sleeping bag; nights at 4,000 m are cold even in August.
Expect crowded trails near the temple; follow your guide, keep together in the dark and respect pilgrims making offerings.

faqs.a: On Janai Purnima, the full moon of Shrawan, usually in August, with Malika Chaturdashi celebrated on the eve. Pilgrims arrive over several days before. The date follows the lunar calendar and changes each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days does it take to reach the Badimalika fair?
faqs.a: From Martadi, the Bajura headquarters, the trek takes three to four days to the temple via Triveni Dham. Reaching Martadi from Dhangadhi takes a long day by road. Plan ten to fourteen days in total from Kathmandu, with spare days for monsoon delays.

faqs.q: Can foreigners attend the Badimalika fair?
faqs.a: Yes. Respectful foreign visitors are welcome, though very few make the journey. Travel with a licensed agency and guide, follow the priests' and pilgrims' customs at the temple, ask before photographing, and be prepared for basic conditions and large crowds.

faqs.q: Is there mobile coverage at Badimalika during the fair?
faqs.a: Nepal Telecom installed a 4G tower in the Badimalika area ahead of the Janai Purnima fair, so there is now coverage near the temple, though it may be patchy and congested. Carry a satellite messenger or agree emergency plans with your guide as a backup.
